content.text: An Effect is for keeping something outside React in sync, not for reacting to your own state. If a value can be calculated from props or state, calculate it during render. If code runs because the user did something, put it in that event's handler. Both are shorter than the Effect, never go stale, and skip an extra render.

Two bug reports arrive from the shop on the same day. The first: "I removed a pair of shoes from my cart and it said 'Added to cart'." The second: "That toast also pops up every time I open the cart page." Both come from one innocent Effect that shows the toast whenever the cart's items change. Right above it sits another Effect that recalculates the total the same way. Neither one talks to anything outside React, and that's the real problem.
The common misconception

The belief: when some state changes and something else should follow, an Effect is the place for it. Items changed? An Effect updates the total. The cart grew? An Effect shows a toast. The dependency array reads like a list of triggers: "when this changes, do that".
It's an easy habit to form. Effects are the one Hook whose job sounds like "run code when something changes", and writing the Effect keeps every reaction in one tidy place. In a class component,
componentDidUpdate

was where you compared old and new values and acted on the difference, so the pattern feels familiar. And it works, in the sense that the screen ends up right. The costs show up as extra renders, a value that's briefly stale, and logic that fires for reasons nobody intended.
What actually happens
Ask two questions before writing an Effect
React's docs call
Effects

an escape hatch: they're for synchronizing with a system outside React, like a network connection, a browser API or a non-React widget. If there's no outside system, you usually don't need one. When you're not sure, ask why the code needs to run. If it's because the component is now on screen, an Effect fits. If it's because the user clicked, typed or submitted something, the code belongs in that event's handler.
Derived values: calculate, don't store
A total, a filtered list or a full name made of two fields is
derived state

: it can be calculated from props or existing state. React's docs are blunt about it: if you can calculate it during rendering, don't put it in state. Copying it into state with an Effect costs a full extra pass. React renders the component and its children with the old total, commits, runs the Effect, which sets the new total, and renders everything again. You also now have two sources of truth that only agree after the Effect has run.
Calculated in the component body, the total is recomputed on every render from the current items, so it's never stale and needs no dependency list. If the calculation is genuinely slow, wrap it in
useMemo
, which caches the result until its inputs change. It's still a calculation during render, not an Effect.
Event logic: let the cause decide
An Effect only sees state after the fact. It knows that
items

changed, not whether the user added an item, removed one, or just opened a page with a saved cart. That's why the toast lies. The message belongs to one specific action, so it goes in that action's handler, where the cause is known:

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
✅ Right

content.text: The right version has one state variable instead of two and no Effects. Removing an item can't show "Added to cart" any more, because only
add
shows it, and opening the page shows nothing because no handler ran. Code caused by the component being on screen, like logging a page view, is still a fine Effect. Code caused by a click is not.

An Effect that sets state, which triggers another Effect that sets more state, renders the tree once per link. It's also fragile: set one piece of state from somewhere new, like an undo button, and the whole chain fires again. Compute all the next state in the event handler instead, using local variables, since state is a snapshot until the next render.
Store less, derive the rest
Many "sync" Effects exist because state holds a copy of something. A classic one clears the selection when the list changes:
useEffect(() => setSelected(null), [orders])
. React's guide on state structure suggests storing only the selected id and finding the item during render with
orders.find((o) => o.id === selectedId) ?? null
. The selection then follows the latest data and becomes
null
by itself when the order disappears. The same goes for props: copying a prop into state freezes its first value. Use the prop directly, or name it
initialItems
, as above, when ignoring later values is the point.

rows.text: Sets state calculated from other props or state
Resets all of a component's state when a prop changes
Clears or fixes a selection when the list changes
Store the selected id and derive the item
Reacts to state a click just set: a toast, a POST, navigation
Do it in that click's event handler
Call it in the same handler that sets the state

content.text: Wrap the calculation in
console.time("total")
and
console.timeEnd("total")
. React's docs suggest that around 1 ms or more is where
useMemo
starts to make sense. Measure in a production build with CPU throttling, since development builds are slower and Strict Mode renders twice.

Subscribing to a socket, controlling a map or video widget, and fetching data that must match the current props are all synchronization with something outside React. Those stay Effects, with proper cleanup.
How to apply it in your project

items.title: Find Effects that only call setters

content.text: Search for
useEffect
bodies that just call
setSomething
from other props or state, or let the
set-state-in-effect
rule in the recommended
eslint-plugin-react-hooks
preset flag them. Each is a candidate for a calculation in render, a
key
, or an id instead of a copy.

If the honest answer is "because the user clicked, typed or submitted", move the code to that handler. Keep the Effect only if the answer is "because this is on screen" or "to stay in sync with something outside React".
Store ids instead of copied objects, drop state that mirrors props, and merge values that always change together. Less state means fewer things to keep in sync.
Unless you're creating or looping over thousands of objects, a calculation in render is rarely expensive. Add
useMemo
where a measurement says so, or let React Compiler handle it.
Key takeaways

items.text: If a value can be calculated from props or state, calculate it during render instead of copying it with an Effect.
Effects see that state changed, not why; code caused by a user action belongs in that action's handler.
Store the minimum state, like ids instead of copies, and reset whole components with a
Keep Effects for synchronizing with systems outside React, such as sockets, widgets and browser APIs.
